cards.back: The study of matter and the changes that it undergoes.
A type of scientific investigation that seeks to gain knowledge for the sake of knowledge itself.
A type of scientific investigation that is undertaken to solve a specific problem.
The amount of matter in an object.
Matter that has a definite composition; also known as a chemical weight.
A defined unit in a system of measurement based on an object or event in the physical world and independent of other units.
The SI base unit for time.
The SI base unit for length.
The SI base unit for mass.
The SI base unit of temperature.
A unit defined by a combination of base units.
The metric unit for volume equal to one cubic decimeter (1L = dm^3; 1L = 1,000 mL; 0.001 L = 1 mL).
The amount of mass per unit volume; a physical property.
Expresses any number as a number between 1 and 10 (coefficient) multiplied by 10 raised to a power (exponent).
A systematic approach to problem solving that uses conversion factors to move from one unit to another.
A ratio of equivalent values used to express the same quantity in different units; is always equal to 1 and changes the units without changing its value.
Data that measures using numbers (e.g., 100 mL of vinegar).
Data that uses words (e.g., red, shiny).
Time: seconds (s), Length: meter (m), Mass: kilogram (kg), Temperature: kelvin (k), Amount of substance: mole (mol), Electric current: ampere (A), Luminous intensity: candela (cd).
K to C: K - 273.
C to K: C + 273.
A base unit is a single defined unit; a derived unit combines two base units together.
m^3 (can also be measured in cm^3 or liters; 1L = 1,000 mL, 1L = 1,000 cm^3).
meters per second (m/s).

If you move the decimal point to the right, the exponent will be NEGATIVE; if you move it to the left, it will be POSITIVE.
Coefficient must be between 1 and 10.
The exponents MUST be the SAME, just add/subtract the coefficients.
Multiply coefficients and add exponents (exponents do not have to be the same).
Divide coefficients and subtract exponents (exponents do not have to be the same).
The result will always be 1; if a number is multiplied by 10^0, the result stays the same (e.g., 5^0 = 1 and 5.2 × 10^0 = 5.2).
The same units should be across each other: one in the numerator of one factor and the other in the denominator of the other factor.
Cancel like units until you are left with the target unit and evaluate the remaining factor(s).
How close a measured value is to an accepted value (known value).
How close a series of measurements are to each other.
Error = experimental value - accepted value.
| error | / accepted value * 100.
Errors that consistently affect results.
Errors that randomly appear.
Natural human mistakes.
Nonzero #s are always significant (e.g., 7.23 g has 3 sig figs).
All final 0s to the right of the decimal point are always significant (e.g., 6.20 has 3 sig figs).
Any 0 between 2 sig figs are significant (e.g., 60.5 has 3 sig figs).
Placeholder 0s are not significant—remove them by rewriting in scientific notation (e.g., 0.0253 and 4320 have 3 each).
Counting #s and defined constants have an infinite number of significant figures (e.g., 6 molecules, 60 seconds = 1 minute).
Leading 0s (before non-zero #s for decimals only) and trailing zeros (after non-zero #s for whole #s only; if it is a decimal, rule #2 applies) are both placeholder 0s.
Shows percentages/parts of a fixed whole (aka pie chart).
Shows how a quantity varies across categories.
In chemistry, points represent the intersection of data for 2 variables: independent and dependent.
The variable that you change in your experiment; plotted on the x-axis.
The variable that depends on the independent variable; plotted on the y-axis.
Slope = rise/run = ∆y/∆x = (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1).
(+) slope means both independent and dependent variables increase; (-) slope means the independent variable increases and the dependent variable decreases.
The line that contains most of the plotted data points after you draw through/near the trend.
The amount of space an object takes up.
Amount of matter in an object.
